title: Puppy Socialization Checklist: What to Introduce and How to Do It Safely
description: A puppy socialization checklist with safe ideas for before and after vaccines, how to go at your puppy's pace, how to pick a class, and when to get help.
excerpt: What to introduce your puppy to, before and after vaccines, and how to keep it calm, from veterinary behaviorists and Dogs Trust.
seoTitle: Puppy Socialization Checklist: What to Do First
imageAlt: PuppyGuido article cover: Puppy Socialization Checklist: What to Introduce and How to Do It Safely
html:
Socialization means giving your puppy calm, positive first experiences with the people, sounds, places and animals they will meet in life. The sources agree you should start as soon as your puppy comes home, but they differ on when to go out and when to start classes, so ask your vet. Go at your puppy's pace and stop if they look worried.

When does socialization matter most?

Sources give slightly different windows:

SourceWindow
AVSAB (veterinary behaviorists)The first three months of life are the most important time.
VCAAbout 3 to 16 weeks.
AKCGenerally about 5 to 16 weeks.
Dogs TrustThe first four months.

All of them say to start as soon as your puppy joins your family. AVSAB says to keep going after three months, and to keep offering new experiences through the first year. Dogs Trust says puppies who are overwhelmed or have negative experiences early are more likely to be worried as adults, which is why the goal is calm, not "as much as possible."

What about before vaccines?

This is where sources differ, so read carefully and ask your vet.

  • At home, right away. Dogs Trust says to start as soon as your puppy joins your family, using things around the house (see the checklist).
  • Going out. Dogs Trust says puppies should not walk in public places before they are fully vaccinated, and to ask your vet how long to wait after vaccination. It also says your puppy should start an anti-parasite routine before going out. You can carry your puppy in a carrier or sling.
  • Classes. AVSAB says puppies can start classes as early as 7 to 8 weeks, after at least one set of vaccines given 7 or more days before the first class and a first deworming, and that they should stay up to date. AVSAB says socialization before full vaccination should be the standard of care for puppies.
  • Places to avoid. AVSAB says to avoid dog parks and busy areas used by dogs of unknown vaccination or health status.

Ground rules

  • Let your puppy set the pace. Dogs Trust: always go at your puppy's pace.
  • Stop if worried. Dogs Trust says to stop if your puppy looks worried or moves away, or if they seem highly excited.
  • Reward every time. Dogs Trust suggests rewards and something enjoyable to do.
  • Stay calm and interested. VCA says to make sure your puppy remains calm and interested, and to protect young puppies from fear-provoking situations.
  • Never force it. Go back to an easier step if your puppy is unsure (Dogs Trust).
  • Keep it positive. AVSAB says classes and home training should be based on positive reinforcement.

The checklist

Tick items off when your puppy has had a calm, positive experience. Items marked ★ wait until your vet says it is safe to go out.

People

  • ☐ People of different ages, backgrounds and walks of life (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Someone in a big hat, with a walking stick, an umbrella, a rucksack or a high-vis jacket (Dogs Trust suggests props at home)
  • ☐ The doorbell (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Being handled gently by many people (AVSAB: handling of all body parts)

Sounds and household

  • ☐ Everyday home sounds, with fireworks and other loud noises introduced using recordings (Dogs Trust suggests sound recordings)
  • ☐ The vacuum cleaner and hairdryer, first switched off, then on (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Everyday smells around the home, not near their bed or bowls (Dogs Trust)

Surfaces and objects

  • ☐ Different floor surfaces (Dogs Trust, AVSAB)
  • ☐ Bicycles, suitcases, wheelchairs, buggies (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Tunnels, steps and safe toys to explore (AVSAB)

Handling and the vet

  • ☐ Paws, ears, nails and coat being touched, like at the vet or groomer (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ A calm vet visit (ask your vet about timing)

Travel

  • ☐ Climbing in and out of the car, wearing a harness, with the engine running (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Car trips (AVSAB says puppies should accompany owners on as many car trips as possible)

Alone time and rest

  • ☐ Short periods alone (Dogs Trust). See our guide to leaving a puppy alone.
  • ☐ Playing alone with a stuffed food toy, and napping in a safe place such as a crate or pen (AVSAB). See the nap and sleep schedule and the crate training guide.

Animals ★

  • ☐ Other dogs of all ages, shapes and sizes, once your puppy is fully vaccinated (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Cats, horses and farm animals, seen from a distance, for example walking past a field (Dogs Trust)

Going out ★

  • ☐ First walks, once your vet says it is safe (Dogs Trust)
  • ☐ Busy, calm places, at your puppy's pace

Meeting other dogs

Dogs Trust suggests these steps, starting once your puppy is fully vaccinated:

  1. Walk calmly on a loose lead and reward it.
  2. Keep your distance from other dogs and reward attention on you.
  3. Move slowly closer.
  4. Walk alongside a friend's dog, both on lead.
  5. If both dogs are relaxed, let them say hello and sniff, then keep moving on lead.
  6. Only allow off-lead play when your puppy is happy and has a reliable recall. See first commands to teach a puppy.

If your puppy seems unsure, go back to the stage where they were relaxed.

Choosing a puppy class

  • Ask your vet. AVSAB says each puppy should have up-to-date vaccinations and be free of disease and parasites. It suggests classes held on surfaces that are easy to clean and disinfect, such as indoors.
  • Positive methods. AVSAB and AKC both favor positive reinforcement.
  • Watch first. AKC suggests watching a class without your dog. Does the instructor give each dog equal time? Do the students look like they are having fun?

Fear and tricky moments

Dogs Trust says to stop if your puppy looks worried. AKC describes a first fear period around 8 to 11 weeks and a second between 6 and 14 months, generally lasting no more than two weeks. During these times AKC suggests:

  • Short, fun sessions
  • Lowering the criteria for success, for example rewarding a step toward something rather than touching it
  • Not using treats to lure a fearful puppy closer
  • Avoiding busy, overstimulating outings

If your puppy seems fearful of new situations, AKC suggests a professional trainer who specializes in fear, and a vet visit to rule out health problems. VCA says puppies that show fear need a customized plan and benefit from professional guidance. AVSAB says owners of puppies displaying fear should seek veterinary guidance.

When to ask a professional

  • Your puppy is regularly scared, freezes, hides or tries to escape
  • Fear is getting worse, or lasts beyond a short phase
  • You are unsure what is safe before vaccines are finished

Ask your vet first. This article is general information, not veterinary advice.

quick: Start at home as soon as your puppy arrives, keep experiences calm and positive, and stop if your puppy looks worried. Sources differ on when to go out and start classes before vaccines are complete, so ask your vet.

faq.q: When should I start socializing my puppy?
faq.a: As soon as your puppy comes home, according to Dogs Trust. Start at home and ask your vet about going out.

faq.q: Can I socialize before vaccines are complete?
faq.a: Sources say yes at home. AVSAB says it should be the standard of care, and that classes can start after at least one vaccine set and deworming. Dogs Trust says not to walk in public places until fully vaccinated. Ask your vet.

faq.q: Can I carry my puppy outside?
faq.a: Dogs Trust suggests carrying your puppy in a carrier or sling.
AVSAB says to avoid dog parks and other busy areas with dogs of unknown vaccination or health status.

faq.q: How many new things should my puppy meet each day?
faq.a: We did not find a source with a number. Keep it calm and stop if your puppy looks worried.

faq.q: What if I missed the window?
faq.a: AVSAB says owners of puppies past three months should keep socializing as much as practical. If your puppy shows fear, ask your vet.
